#867. Liverpool and Van Dijk have a decision to make

Virgil van Dijk joined Liverpool for Â£75m from Southampton in January 2018

After Liverpool beat Brighton in October, Virgil van Dijk went upstairs to one of the hospitality lounges at Anfield and met up with Alan Hansen.

It was Van Dijk who, at the end of the 2024-25 season, asked the former Liverpool and Scotland defender to present him with the Premier League trophy and this time they posed for a picture that inevitably did the rounds on social media.

Whenever the time comes for Van Dijk to move on from Liverpool, he will go down as arguably their greatest centre-half, alongside Hansen. The question now is whether he will finish his career at Anfield like Hansen did in 1991.

Van Dijk's contract expires next summer and, even if the 35-year-old insisted this week that he was in no panic, it is a topic that will be a source of debate until a decision is made.

"Let's see what the season brings. I've had an amazing time already so far. If that will be extended, that's the case. If not, then I will go somewhere else," the Liverpool captain told reporters at Selhurst Park.

Two seasons ago, with Van Dijk in a similar situation, there was a similar sense of calm and come April 2025 he signed a two-year-deal.

Judging by Van Dijk's comments there is a feeling of him wanting to stay, but both he and Liverpool have an important decision to make.

Van Dijk and Alan Hansen are regarded as two of Liverpool's greatest defenders

Aside from a poor error against Villarreal in the Champions League, Van Dijk has shown this season that his standards haven't dropped.

His partnership with Jeremy Jacquet, who joined in the summer, is going from strength to strength and Van Dijk has played every minute in the Premier League since the start of last season.

A "little niggle" has affected him in recent weeks and this is the first international window he has missed with the Netherlands since Euro 2020, but it isn't a major cause for concern.

Liverpool have lost a number of senior figures in recent years but Van Dijk remains a leader in every form, and that was evidenced by his suggestion to Andoni Iraola that the squad should visit the museum at Anfield to learn more about the club's history.

At Crystal Palace on Sunday, it spoke volumes of Van Dijk's character that he came over to a group of reporters and asked if they wanted to speak to him, rather than the other way around. He regularly fronts up, regardless of the result.

Van Dijk is certainly not the force he was under Jurgen Klopp but he remains an elite centre-half and the stats justify that.

Per 90 minutes this season in the Premier League, he averages 60.7 successful passes per game, wins possession 3.5 times and makes 7.1 clearances. He has a 75% success in duels and 79% when it comes to aerial duels.

In his first full season at the club, in 2018-19, he averaged 72.4 successful passes per game, won possession 5.1 times and made 5.3 clearances. He had a 76% success in duels and 75% when it came to aerial duels.

That said, the Liverpool hierarchy will have seen the way the situation with Mohamed Salah unfolded last year and will be keen to avoid a repeat. After a stellar season in 2024-25, Salah's numbers plummeted in 2025-26.

Liverpool have a number of young centre-backs within their ranks, from Jacquet and Giovanni Leoni to the likes of Ifeanyi Ndukwe and Mor Talla Ndiaye, but letting Van Dijk go would be a risk and leave a gaping hole.

He didn't take a pay cut in 2025 and continues to earn a salary understood to be in the region of Â£400,000 a week.

Joe Gomez, 29, is also out of contract this summer and Liverpool do have an option to buy Ronald Araujo, 27, at the end of the season from Barcelona but there would be a clear loss of experience and leadership if Van Dijk leaves.

For sporting director Julian Ward, the future of the Dutchman will be a priority over the coming months.

Providing he is fit, Van Dijk will make his 390th appearance for Liverpool when they take on Manchester United after the international break.

And given his consistency, he is likely to reach 400 appearances by the end of the year. He would become only the 28th Liverpool player to do so.

The 31 goals he has scored for Liverpool in the Premier League is the most for a defender at the club.

In terms of a resolution with his contract, this is likely to be one where both parties bide their time and, given that the existing relationships are strong and there's a mutual respect, it would not be a surprise to see negotiations go into 2027.

Come January, Van Dijk will be able to sign a pre-contract agreement with an overseas club and as such, AC Milan and Juventus are monitoring the situation.

Sources in Turkey are also hopeful that they could tempt him to make the same move as Salah if an extension isn't agreed at Liverpool but, as it stands, it would be quite a surprise if Van Dijk moved on this summer.

#866. RHOP’s Karen Huger Shares Update on Ray Huger Marriage After Season 11

Real Housewives of Potomac's Karen Huger exclusively told E! News at the Hunting Wives season two premiere where she stands with husband Ray Huger as they plan the holidays with daughter Rayvin.

Karen Huger has no illusions of grandeur about the future of her marriage.

While the Real House of Potomac's Grand Dame admitted viewers would have to stay tuned to see how she and husband Ray Huger continue to work on their relationship during season 11, she confessed issues with her partner of 32 years haven't gone away.

"We're going through a rough patch," Karen exclusively told E! News at the Hunting Wives season two premiere Nov. 12, crediting her ability to face their struggles to the fact that "Ray and I have always been honest."

And despite the difficulties in her relationship since her return home after serving six months in prison due to a 2024 DUI conviction, the reality star has a positive outlook about their family unit with daughter Rayvin Huger.

As Karen explained, "The one thing is, we will always be a family, and we will always be friends."

And because of the couple's unbreakable bond, their plans for the holidays remain a family affair where the motto is the more the merrier.

"We're going to celebrate as a family," Karen shared. "In fact, we are going down to Virginia, near the guest house that I just renovated, to celebrate with our entire family."

As for how the 63-year-old feels about her equally complicated relationship with costar Wendy Osefo?

"I'm hoping for the best for Wendy. I'm always in her corner," Karen remarked. "We are supporting her 100 percent and wishing for the best."

Aside from her Bravo friend group, Karen is also a big fan of the women of Maple Brook, Texas, with the second season of Hunting Wives arriving on Netflix Nov. 26. In fact, she effused about her favorite actress in the drama, Brittany Snow.

As Karen put it, "Brittany Snow? Love, love, love. Sign me up. I'm ready to kill someone, OK."

With that in mind, Karen is open to trying out her acting chops alongside the Hunting Wives cast, musing when it comes to a future cameo, "All things are possible."

Read on for more fan-worthy TV series premiering in 2026.

Nocturne tells the story of Jonah Lynn (Liev Schreiber), an ex-soldier turned homicide detective who, tired of working the tough streets of Philadelphia, moves to a small town in Western Pennsylvania for a quiet life. But, as the town and his family come under attack from the diabolically cunning serial killer Jurek Walter (Stephen Graham), Jonah must protect all that he holds dear. When the desperate search for Jurek’s last missing victim forces Jonah to send his surrogate daughter FBI Agent Saga Bauer (Zazie Beetz) up against Jurek, how far will Jonah go?

Bertha Russell changed Society at a cost. Now, her family must reckon with the consequences as Agnes van Rhijn seizes an opportunity to regain her position. Meanwhile, Marian forges a new path for herself, and Peggy works to be accepted by her future in-laws. In this new era, you must be careful what you wish for.

St. Denis Medical is a mockumentary about an underfunded, understaffed Oregon hospital where the dedicated doctors and nurses try their best to treat patients while maintaining their own sanity. In season three, romantic entanglements and personal struggles complicate relationships in the Emergency Department, pushing some St. Denis employees to the brink.

The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins (NBC) - Nov. 2

Season two of the hit comedy returns with the unlikely duo of former football star Reggie Dinkins (Tracy Morgan) and documentarian Arthur Tobin (Daniel Radcliffe), both still chasing redemption and still making a mess of it. With the help of his family, Reggie will continue his quest to recapture his past glory.

In season two, Santi takes the next step in his pursuit of professional golf, only to discover how quickly the game changes when talent becomes expectation. As Santi chases his dream, Pryce Cahill (Owen Wilson) finds himself wondering what might still be possible for him. Urged on by his former rival Clark Ross (Timothy Olyphant), Pryce does something nobody expects: he bets on himself, launching an improbable comeback in hopes of becoming the oldest golfer ever to win a major. But the road back proves far harder than he imagined. And the closer Pryce gets to the golfer he once was, the more he is forced to confront why he never fulfilled the promise everyone once saw in him. With brilliant new coach Amanda (Rhea Seehorn) and trusted caddie Mitts (Marc Maron) in his corner, Pryce sets out to prove — to the golf world and, more importantly, to himself — that maybe he really was as good as everyone always said he was.

The lawyers of Grant, Ronson & Greene are back for another season of scandals, secrets, and stilettos. As new allegiances form, friendships are tested and a shocking revelation threatens the very existence of the firm.

The Remarried Princess (Hulu & Disney+) - Nov. 4

Based on the hit Naver Webtoon of the same name, The Remarried Empress follows the strained relationship of beloved Empress Navier and her husband Emperor Sovieshu of the Eastern Kingdom. With anxieties rising across the kingdom, the couple’s relationship begins to fracture when Sovieshu falls in love with a runaway slave and attempts to move heaven and earth to win her heart. Unwilling to compromise her dignity, Navier acquiesces to the emperor’s requests on one condition – that she be allowed to remarry rival Crown Prince Heinrey of the Western Kingdom. What follows is a tale of love, lust and regret that threatens the fate of an entire kingdom as Navier strives to reclaim her power.

The documentary traces Muhammad Ali’s coming of age story, following a young Cassius Clay through the personal, professional and political battles he fought inside and outside the ring. Set against a changing America, The Greatest follows a once-in-a-generation talent fighting for the right to become his own man. Through the fights that made him a champion and the convictions that made him an icon, a young man from Louisville transforms himself into Muhammad Ali, the greatest of all time.

Taken: Natalee Holloway (Netflix) - Nov. 4

On May 30, 2005, 18-year-old Natalee Holloway vanished on a high school graduation trip to Aruba—and never came home. What followed was years of unanswered questions, a missing teenager, and a mother's relentless fight for the truth. Now, over 20 years later, Natalee's mother, Beth, is ready to tell the complete story. With exclusive, unprecedented access to Beth and those who were with Natalee when she vanished, this three-part documentary series is the definitive account of a case that gripped a nation and never let go. It's a story of a mother who refused to stop searching, an investigation that spanned continents, and a daughter whose memory endures. This is Natalee's story, told at last in full.

Helen (Keira Knightley) is still betraying her nation’s secrets to the covert organization she serves: the Black Doves. But after the misadventures of last Christmas, and with her husband Wallace (Andrew Buchan), preparing to become Prime Minister, she is walking a more treacherous line than ever.

Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook (Apple TV) - Nov. 6

The eight-episode series follows Nora Lum, aka Awkwafina, on a cross-country culinary road trip as she attempts to revive her family’s beloved Chinese restaurant.

Wolves Up Close With Bertie Gregory (National Geographic) - Nov. 6

Reconnecting with a pack of wolves he has followed for seven years, Bertie Gregory sets out to capture one of the Arctic’s most dangerous and rarely filmed hunts: wolves taking on a bull moose, prey roughly ten times their size. Led by Kona, a striking white breeding male, the pack faces a critical winter as dwindling food supplies, an encroaching rival wolf and an aging leader threaten its survival.

Charmed By a Southern Monster (Peacock) - Nov. 9

Starring Craig Conover as Hunter Caldwell and Nicole Mattox as Maeve Marchant, the series blends soapy romance, workplace rivalry and small-town mystery.

The story follows Maeve, a brilliant corporate fixer sent to convince and seduce Hunter, a rumored murderer, into selling his family’s estate. But when she discovers that the town’s most feared man may actually be its most misunderstood, and the only person who can protect her from her dangerous ex-boyfriend, Maeve becomes entangled in Hunter’s world. As family secrets and a billion-dollar development deal threaten to unravel their growing connection, she must confront her past and decide how much she’s willing to risk for love.

Whitney Way Thore is stepping into a transformative new chapter. Back in her home state of North Carolina, Whitney has found love with Jake, a man she first met years ago before reconnecting after her return to Charlotte. As their relationship deepens, Whitney is rediscovering her confidence through dance, exploring new possibilities on her health journey, and taking meaningful steps toward the future she’s always wanted, including her biggest dream of becoming a mom.

Picking up after the gut-wrenching mid-series finale, Tony Baddingham and Declan O'Hara's battle for the Cotswolds crown reaches fever pitch, while Rupert Campbell-Black is forced to confront his own personal demons. Against a backdrop of hedonistic parties, Bonfire Night chaos, the Hampshire Hunt Ball and a turbulent Christmas, affairs unravel, alliances fracture and rivalries intensify. Caught in the middle of the frenzied franchise war, Taggie O'Hara must find the courage to follow her heart, while those around her face the consequences of ambition, power and secrets that can no longer remain hidden. But as series two draws to a close, who will get their happy ending?

From Ron Howard, the documentary explores the life, career, and cultural impact of legendary American photographer Richard Avedon.

The Good Daughter is a suspenseful thriller wrapped in a deeply emotional story about love, family and resilience. Sisters Charlotte (Meghann Fahy) and Samantha (Rose Byrne) Quinn have spent the last 20 years trying to piece together the lives that were fractured by a single night of violence. When another attack splinters the small town of Pikeville, Charlotte – now a lawyer like her father – is the first witness on the scene. As the case unfolds and twists through painful memories and buried secrets, what emerges is not just a story of survival, but of enduring ties between a father and his daughters, and the complex bond between sisters.

After a reunion where the status of friendships and situationships remained ambiguous, the Charmers are determined to define their relationships and mend wounds. However, when true feelings bubble up and juicy rumors catch fire, the group seeks to unveil the truth – even if it costs them more than just friendships.

Three years into their jobs as response officers, Constables Grace Ellis, Tommy Foster, and Annie Conlon are operating at their limit, facing a new threat on the streets that the police can barely control. Meanwhile the murder trial of Gerry Cliff exposes a dangerous and long-buried secret that leads to chaos both inside the police, and across the criminal underworld. As they grapple with big decisions about their future, Grace, Tommy and Annie must find the courage to face the greatest threat they have ever encountered: the truth.

Each episode of the drama unfolds across three timelines of a heist: the 12 months of planning, the 12 hours of the heist, and the 12 days following the heist. The series follows a disgraced FBI agent (Anthony Mackie) and an American career criminal (Jamie Dornan) who play a zero-sum game of cat and mouse across Europe. At the center of it all is the daring, epic raid on a bank vault deep beneath the streets of Zurich.

Expedition: Saving Our Seas (National Geographic) - Nov. 13

The documentary follows teams of National Geographic Explorers as they investigate our global Ocean, from seashore to seafloor and pole to pole. Combining cutting-edge technology with the knowledge of coastal communities, they chase the discoveries and solutions needed to protect our Oceans at a critical moment.

Homicide for the Holidays (Oxygen) - Nov. 14

The holidays are supposed to be the most wonderful time of the year. But for some families, cherished celebrations become the backdrop for unimaginable violence. Season six of Homicide For The Holidays brings a new batch of deadly deeds to the supposed jolliest time of the year as investigators pursue those responsible and seek justice for families shattered at a time meant for togetherness.

Diane Morgan returns as Philomena Cunk in a new series from Charlie Brooker. Billed as Cunk's most glamorous outing yet, she charts the history of cinema, from the invention of the camera and the New Wave filmmakers of the 1960s right up to the entrance of CGI and what the future of AI holds. Cunk will attempt to demystify it all while sitting in lumpy seats with stale popcorn, asking herself where did cinema come from? And why? What does it want? And why can’t it tell us?

Small Town Trouble: Texas (Bravo) - Nov. 18

Set in Boerne (pronounced "Bur-nee"), Texas, the series follows a charming yet unconventional group of wives, mothers and social insiders – Aaryn Williams, Alli McAnelly, Annari Uys, Gabby Hernandez Huffman, and Hailey Head, alongside their respective husbands – as conservative values of small-town life collide with forbidden attraction, messy friendships, and shocking   secrets. Here, perception is everything, temptation is everywhere, and the truth is never as buttoned-up as it looks.

The story of Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison, two hyper-smart, ambitious young idealists who tried to remake the global financial system in the blink of an eye - before they were accused of stealing $8 billion and became Gen Z's own Bonnie & Clyde.

Nelly and Ashanti: We Belong Together (Peacock) - Nov. 19

This season, Ashanti continues to balance motherhood, continuing to perform on stage, and taking control of her musical legacy. While navigating living in St. Louis and New York City, Ashanti also juggles re-recording her debut album to retain her masters, finding time for her girlfriends who keep her grounded, and recording new music with some of music's hottest artists. After years of nonstop touring, Nelly reflects on the physical toll it’s taking at this stage in his life, and an unexpected family loss reminds him what matters most. Between raising their son, honoring their village, and planning for their future, Nelly and Ashanti discover that belonging together isn’t about standing still; it’s about building a future on their own terms.

Nearly a decade after a mysterious female jogger dubbed “The Mad Pooper” captured national attention for repeatedly defecating on residential lawns across Colorado Springs, one of the strangest unsolved mysteries is back in the spotlight. In the new two-hour special, viewers will dive headfirst into the bizarre true story that left an entire community searching for answers and asking one simple question: why?

As the survivors race to bury their sins before rescue arrives and an old flame roars back into town with plans of her own, turns out not every homecoming is a joyous one, and this one's going to sting.

Adapted from Tom Bradby's bestselling novel, Secret Service follows senior MI6 officer Kate Henderson (Gemma Arterton), whose covert investigation uncovers evidence that a high-ranking U.K. politician may be working as a Russian asset. With trust shattered and her career on the line, Kate must navigate the shifting sands of political loyalty, international threat, and personal sacrifice as she races to uncover their identity before it's too late.

The new comedy follows a team of dedicated archaeologists (and less-dedicated college students) who spend their summer working on a dig site in Greece. Their discovery of a rare artifact sends them on the adventure of a lifetime.

#864. Fernandes rejects second Man Utd contract offer

Bruno Fernandes joined Manchester United from Sporting in 2020

Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes has rejected a second contract offer from the club.

The Portugal midfielder is out of contract at the end of the season, though the club have the option to trigger a 12-month extension until 2028.

United are keen to avoid that eventuality by extending the 32-year-old's existing deal and have been in talks with the Portuguese's representatives in recent months.

But sources have told BBC Sport that Fernandes has rejected the club's second proposal over a new deal at Old Trafford.

Should United fail to agree a fresh deal with Fernandes, it is almost certain that the club will trigger a 12-month extension in his contract before 1 January.

How Ferguson-inspired Pochettino can succeed where Carrick failed at Man Utd

At that point, the midfielder would be able to sign a pre-contract agreement with foreign clubs as his contract would be within six months of expiring.

It is unclear when Fernandes turned down the offer, but it appears unlikely that a resolution is imminent given the upheaval at the club.

Michael Carrick was sacked as head coach on Thursday following the club's worst start to a domestic campaign in 40 years.

USA coach Mauricio Pochettino is expected to replace Carrick, with the Argentine set to be in charge for the first time when United travel to Anfield to face rivals Liverpool on 22 November.

United will be hoping that Pochettino's arrival will persuade Fernandes to commit his future to the club.

Fernandes came close to joining Pochettino's Tottenham in 2019 but a move failed to materialise, with the midfielder signing for United six months later.

The former Sporting midfielder has scored six times in 13 matches for United this season.

In theory, the current contract stand-off between Manchester United and Bruno Fernandes is not a big deal.

It is usual for the first, second and sometimes quite a few more offers to be rejected as part of the rough and tumble of negotiations.

United do have the option to trigger an option to add an extra year. However, there is reason why both sides might be wary to commit beyond that at this stage.

On Fernandes' part, there is a clear desire to compete for the biggest prizes. He can see the best years of his career drifting away. Yet again United have failed to build on a season of promise and he will now be wanting to see what impact Mauricio Pochettino has when he eventually arrives from the United States.

Fernandes was coveted by the Saudi Pro League 18 months ago, although the feeling has been he would prefer to stay in Europe.

On United's side, they will have noted Fernandes' alarming drop-off from the levels he hit last season, when he broke the Premier League assists record and won all the major player of the year honours.

Liverpool committed a huge amount of money to Mohamed Salah's last contract and that turned out to be a heavy financial burden. United will not want to get saddled with a major contract over an extended period for an underperforming player.

#863. France put injuries behind them to stun Springboks

Tries: Grandidier-Nkanang (15), Attissogbe (24), Bielle-Biarrey (32) Conversions: Lucu (16,24,33)

Tries: Wessels (30), Reinach (51), Marx (72) Conversions: Feinberg-Mngomezulu (31,52)

France vs South Africa Nations Championship 8:10pm Friday 13th November

France put a raft of injuries behind them to withstand huge pressure and defeat South Africa 21-19 in a stunning Nations Championship victory in Paris.

The win is only the second for Les Bleus over the Springboks in the last 11 contests, with the hosts playing sensationally in the first half and digging in to survive and get over the line in the second.

Back-three Aaron Grandidier-Nkanang, Théo Attissogbe and Louis Bielle-Biarrey each scored tries in the opening half, with France belying the fact they had to play Antoine Dupont at 10 due to four fly-halves being out injured (Matthieu Jalibert, Romain Ntamack, Thomas Ramos, Antoine Hastoy).

All three tries were converted by Maxime Lucu, with France 21-7 ahead at the half-time break, but the second half proved entirely different.

France - Tries: Grandidier-Nkanang (15), Attissogbe (24), Bielle-Biarrey (32). Cons: Lucu (16,24,33).

South Africa - Tries: Wessels (30), Reinach (51), Marx (72). Cons: Feinberg-Mngomezulu (31,52).

Though South Africa were shown a 20-minute red card to back-row Cobus Wiese for an illegal ruck clear-out, France coughed up sin-bins to Lucu, Grandidier-Nkanang and Régis Montagne - the latter as a result of scrum penalties which kept flowing the visitors' way.

Scrum-half Cobus Reinach and hooker Malcom Marx scored tries in the second half for South Africa - adding to a first-half Jan-Hendrik Wessels effort - but Manie Libbok crucially missed the third conversion and the chance to draw level.

South Africa's wholesale front-row changes less than an hour before kick-off - swapping their starting front-row for their replacements - had ​little impact on France's fast start, with Dupont floating between fly-half and scrum-half from the off in a marvellous individual performance.

The match was considered a potential preview of the final at Twickenham in two weeks, but while France are closing in on representing the northern hemisphere - England and Ireland are now six points behind with two games to play - South Africa may not make it.

The Springboks will be overtaken atop the southern hemisphere standings and lose their No 1 world ranking if undefeated New Zealand beat Wales on Saturday in Cardiff, as expected.

On Friday, the Springboks closed to 21-14 with 30 minutes to go, revving up their power game for a grandstand finish.

France were bleeding penalties - nine in the scrum alone - but desperate scramble defence roused a packed Stade de France.

South Africa's Pieter-Steph du Toit was held up over the try-line late on, while Lucu - France's goalkicker with an 85 per cent success rate - ramped up the tension when he missed a straightforward penalty attempt that would have given France a 10-point lead.

Springboks hooker Marx inevitably scored from a rolling maul but Libbok, on for Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu, botched the conversion attempt that would have levelled the score with eight minutes left.

The Boks had one last chance in the final minute, but Bielle-Biarrey stopped the charge and Dupont jumped on the loose ball, earning Lucu the chance to kick out and end a gripping Test match.

"I feel tired! They [South Africa] are really intense during the 80 minutes.

"It was so hard today with the yellow cards. We kept the intensity the whole game, and that's a huge thing for us today.

"We tried to adapt [Dupont at fly-half], we just had one day of training this week.

"I tried with Max [Lucu] to have the best combination possible. In attack and defence.

"With the energy of the entire team, it worked."

For France, they next face Argentina in their third Nations Championship Test of the autumn at the Stade de France in Paris on Saturday, November 21 (8.10pm kick-off).

South Africa travel to face Ireland at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin for their next Test, also on Saturday November 21 (4.40pm kick-off).

#858. McGinn double seals win for ragged Scotland

Scotland vs North Macedonia. UEFA Nations League Group B1.

Match report as John McGinn scores twice in Scotland's win over North Macedonia at Hampden; Aston Villa midfielder gives hosts lead after McTominay and Gilmour go close; Rastoder's header levels scoring; McGinn penalty seals win after Gannon-Doak fouled; Scotland face Switzerland next

John McGinn's double rescued Scotland as they toiled to a 2-1 win over North Macedonia to keep their Nations League promotion hopes alive.

The hosts were booed off at half-time with the game goalless but there was a sense of relief - rather than joy - at the final whistle after McGinn's penalty secured the three points after Elmin Rastoder's header cancelled out the Aston Villa midfielder's opener.

The win means Scotland can still finish second in Group B1 after Slovenia were held by Switzerland, but will have to win in St Gallen on Monday and hope North Macedonia do them a favour in their final game.

Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli secured his first win at Hampden on a night when skipper Andy Robertson earned his 102nd cap to equal the appearance record held by Sir Kenny Dalglish.

The returning Scott McTominay nearly grabbed an opener after 16 minutes but he was denied by Stole Dimitrievski in the North Macedonia goal after turning and shooting sharply. The keeper then denied Che Adams and McTominay again before the Napoli midfielder attempted to recreate his famous Denmark overhead kick to no avail.

Boos rang around Hampden as the players trudged off at the interval and Billy Gilmour did little to lift the collective mood straight after the break when he fired over with the goal gaping following good work by Adams.

Scotland did take the lead soon after, however, Adams outmuscling his North Macedonian counterpart to set the onrushing McGinn away into the box before he curled his effort into the net.

Rastoder stunned Hampden less than three minutes later, leaping highest to glance his header past Angus Gunn from a corner, but Dimitrievski went from hero to villain with a little over 15 minutes remaining, bringing down Ben Gannon-Doak when the winger seemed to be running the ball out of play.

A VAR review followed, allowing McGinn to step up and deliver a first win in Glasgow for Pocognoli, but it is a performance that will raise more questions than answers.

16: BIG SAVE! Scott McTominay controls the ball with his back to the goal, then turns sharply and shoots but Stole Dimitrievski gets down well to his left and keeps it out.

22: OVER! Andy Robertson delivers a free-kick into the box but Kieran Tierney's header loops over the bar.

27: SAVE! John McGinn's corner is met by Che Adams at the front post before his header takes a big deflection. It looks like it's heading in but Dimitrievski is equal to it again.

35: OVER! McTominay tries an acrobatic effort with an overhead kick but it sails over the bar and out of play.

39: MCTOMINAY DENIED! The ball is threaded into the feet of McTominay and he shoots from a tight angle but the goalkeeper makes another save to keep it level!

46: HOW HAS HE MISSED?! Adams capitalises on a loose back pass and squares the ball to Billy Gilmour. All he has to do is guide it on target and it is a goal but he skies it over the bar!

54: GOAL! Adams outmuscles the defender before poking the ball forward allowing McGinn to race onto it before curling the opener into the back of the net.

57: GOAL! North Macedonia shock Scotland with a quickfire equaliser. The corner is whipped into the box and Rastoder is there to glance it into the bottom corner.

75: GOAL! McGinn scores from the spot to restore Scotland's lead

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"I'm happy to get the first win at home. It's important and we knew before the game that it will help to build a winning culture.

"In terms of what we produced on the pitch, I know exactly what we worked on this week. I'm quite satisfied about what I saw in some moments of the game, the work on the ball and off the ball.

"It was not always perfect, but I know that what we worked on in the last two days happened many times on the pitch. And for me that's very important. On top of that, we created a lot of chances that we should score.

"Off the ball, I think we were quite aggressive. We recovered a number of balls that we managed well in some moments of transition. We created a big chance for Billy (Gilmour) from this also. So that's a new approach of the game. Not everything was perfect, but there was a lot to take to move forward.

"After the first goal, I think we need to learn to not drop the intensity. Because after the first goal, for five minutes, I really feel like we dropped the intensity and the focus. And we conceded a goal from a set-piece. And I had the same feeling after the second goal. So, it's something that we need to fix."

Scotland captain Andy Robertson speaking to BBC Sport:

"I thought we showed glimpses of good stuff. We tried to be patient on the ball, tried to keep the ball, I think we did that well at times, but also at times it broke down because the quality wasn't there at times so we're still trying to piece it all together.

"It's a different way of playing and that's what we are working on in the training ground. It wasn't always perfect, but no international game is easy and we're all delighted in the changing room to get that win and hopefully other people have a smile on their face too.

"Every formation can be played differently, there are so many different variations of this formation. We're trying to implement what the manager and coaches want us to do on the training ground and we're working really hard.

"Yes, it's not going to be perfect right away but everything is working towards us going into the qualifiers for the Euros. We're still trying to learn it and we believe in what the manager is trying to teach us to do and we have to be patient with that.

"I know people don't see us train and see the work we're doing in the background, so I can get why people are frustrated but there is an idea behind what we are doing and like you say at times we lacked that quality.

"Obviously the Slovenia at home game made it unrealistic, or tougher [to qualify]. We'll go over to Monday and we'll give everything we can to win that game. We're in a position where we have to rely on other results."

On equaling Dalglish's appearance record: "It feels amazing for me and my family, it's an amazing achievement. I've been around here for a long time. I've had highs, I've had lows, I've sometimes had praise and had criticism."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

John McGinn to Sky Sports on Andy Robertson's record-equalling night:

"Amazing - he deserves everything that is coming his way. The biggest credit I can give him is that he is always available, always willing to help his country. Whether he is at 60, 70, 80 per cent, or 100.

"I'm sure Monday will be a special occasion for him but he'll give the boring answer that it will only be special if we get three points."

It will be a night that Andy Robertson never forgets but a game most Scotland fans will blank from their collective memories fairly quickly.

The skipper equalled Sir Kenny Dalglish's record of 102 caps but it was fellow Scotland stalwart John McGinn who spared the home side's blushes on a drab evening in Glasgow.

Scotland looked slow in their build-up, even if there were first-half chances, but when the goal finally did come the floodgates did not open. Instead, North Macedonia, who hadn't scored since November 18, 2025, equalised and could have gone in front.

The natives were understandably restless but were ultimately relieved when Stole Dimitrievski clumsily brought down Gannon-Doak, allowing McGinn to be the hero again.

The Aston Villa captain was quick to remind everyone that a new style takes time to bed in and that is true. Scotland are moving away from the comforts and success of the Steve Clarke era, but questions will be asked of Pocognoli's insistence on using wing-backs and one upfront at home with a comfortable win expected.

Scotland have something to play for when they travel to Switzerland for their final Group B1 game, with promotion still up for grabs. Robertson should play on Monday to become Scotland's most-capped player outright. How sweet it would be if his 103rd appearance for his country was a winning one.

#856. I’m Obsessed With UGG’s Ugly-Cute Ballet Sneakers (Others Disagree)

The Quill Ballet Sneakers have divided the E! shopping team, but their cozy lining and easy styling won me over. Here’s how they fit and what to know before buying.

You thought the fashion world was done with ballet sneakers? Think again! These trendy shoes just got a chilly-weather makeover. Introducing the UGG Quill Ballet Sneakers, the cozy winter slipper meets sturdy sole meets delicate pointe shoe in the brand's signature colorways and raw suede edges. In other words... some people love it, and others hate it.

This UGG ballet sneaker has truly divided the E! shopping team, with various team members swearing they're ugly and others who are absolutely obsessed with them. I'm in the latter camp. Let's face it, we don't usually go to UGG for their trendy pieces (although some other flats in their collection might be changing that), we turn to them time and time again for the cozy & casual look, and that's exactly what this shoe provides.

I got the UGG ballet sneakers in the brand's signature chestnut/sand colorway a month ago... and love them. They're so comfortable and so easy to style. I usually pair them with jeans and a casual top or sweater. They're cute in an "ugly" way. They can be worn with or without socks. I'd recommend them with socks if you're walking a lot, and I even prefer the look of them with thick socks. But wearing them with bare feet is also an easy vibe.

When it comes to sizing, I'm usually between sizes 8.5 and 9. The smaller size is for flats, heels, and everything I'd prefer to wear without socks. 9 is reserved for narrow shoes, boots, and low-profile sneakers that have a slimmer fit. For UGG's ballet sneakers, I went with an 8.5, and they're the tiniest bit too big without socks and absolutely perfect with a thick sock.

If you love the coziness of your favorite UGG slipper with the ease of styling a ballet flat and the sturdiness of a sneaker sole, I'd highly recommend the UGG Quill Ballet Sneakers—especially when certain colors are on sale!

In UGG's classic chestnut/sand colorway, these ballet sneakers feature a soft suede upper, lace-up ties that wrap around the ankle, and an ultra-plush natural sheepskin lining.

Prefer a color that goes with everything in your closet? This black colorway is the perfect neutral, with the same features as the classic shade, but with more subtle raw edges on the suede upper.

Chic, while still a colorful neutral, this high-voltage blue colorway of UGG's ballet sneaker is to die for (in this shopping writer's opinion, at least).

If you want a fiery pop of color, this (nearly sold-out) red pepper colorway of the UGG ballet sneaker is a gorgeous, cool-toned red you won't find anywhere else.

#855. Rugby League World Cup finals, ATP and WTA tennis, plus WSL – follow with us

Here’s how to follow along with our coverage – the finest writing and up-to-the-minute reports

Old Trafford and Selhurst Park watchers aside, the break from Premier League events – on the pitch at least – heralds a day of lively international activity. Emillia Hawkins arises bright and early with all the Nations League buildup as Wales, Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland bound into view later. There may well be follow-up from Scotland’s Friday night date with North Macedonia and anticipation for England’s clash with Spain on Sunday. Plus, a host of EFL and WSL fixtures will keep the updates flowing. Join the conversation at matchday.live@theguardian.com.

Greg Wood saddles up for a cracking ‘Super Saturday’ in the autumn’s best meeting, with the Paddy Power Gold Cup Handicap Chase front and centre and Ben Pauling’s Meetmebythesea hard to ignore. Elsewhere, Old Park Star could make a winning start over fences in the Arkle Challenge Trophy Trial Novice Chase.

Simon Burnton helms the blog as the WSL’s two unbeaten sides go head to head at lunchtime. Andrée Jeglertz’s City hold top spot after drubbing West Ham 5-0 while Chelsea were held by Everton last weekend. With two points separating the pacesetters, this is a crucial match for Chelsea – lose and their title hopes will become worryingly untethered even at this stage of the season. Suzanne Wrack reports.

England welcome their former head coach Eddie Jones’s Japan to Allianz Stadium, Twickenham, after delivering their standout performance of an otherwise poor 2026 by overrunning Australia 45-22 in the autumn opener last weekend. Ranked 12th in the world, Japan are not expected to cause Steve Borthwick’s rejigged XV to stumble before the main event of the Nations Championship pool fixtures against New Zealand. This match is of particular significance for Will Joseph, Max Ojomoh and Cadan Murley, who have been told the second of this month’s four Tests is a World Cup audition. Borthwick already knows the bulk of the squad he will pick for Australia 2027, leaving around five spots up for grabs. These fringe places are the hardest to pick and with Japan offering a rare chance for Test rookies to catch Borthwick’s attention, a strong individual display could tip the scales in their favour. Alex Reid hosts the blog, with Robert Kitson and Gerard Meagher reporting.

Scott Murray bids a hearty noswaith dda as Wales attempt to block Erling Haaland and company for the second time in six weeks. Craig Bellamy’s side stunned the World Cup quarter-finalists at the start of October with a shock 2-1 win in Cardiff. They meet again in Oslo, with the bottom two sides in Group A4 aiming to ward off the threat of relegation to League B. Haaland – the Nations League’s all-time top scorer with 22 goals – drew a rare blank at Cardiff City Stadium. On home turf and temperatures around zero degrees centigrade, Wales must hope the Manchester City striker is frozen out once more.

So much for the machinations of Sandpapergate, England were duly humbled in the first ODI against their old foes, crashing to a seven-wicket defeat in Perth on Friday morning. They were bowled out for 131 in 33.4 overs ⁠after losing the toss, ⁠and the hosts ​reached 132 for three in 23.3 overs courtesy of a quickfire 50 by captain Mitch Marsh, with a stunning six for 24 from Mahli Beardman on debut stealing the show. Tim de Lisle logs on with over-by-over commentary of the second ODI as the three-match series moves to Adelaide and concludes in Hobart on Wednesday. Ali Martin reports.

Australia and New Zealand opened the Rugby League World Cup with a humdinger of a contest four weeks ago and hopes are high for another blockbuster when they face off again with ⁠the title on the line in Brisbane. The Kangaroos fullback Reece Walsh ​and his Kiwis counterpart Kalyn Ponga were the stars of the show last month in Sydney, and their pace, footwork and handling should again be vital for their teams in the Lang Park showcase. Australia and New Zealand also meet in the women’s World Cup final earlier on Sunday at the same stadium, where the Jillaroos will be gunning for a fourth straight title against the Kiwi Ferns, who won the first three editions. Join us for live coverage of both finals.

Xaymaca Awoyungbo has breaking news and buildup at the helm of our unbeatable football live blog. He’ll be looking ahead to Spain v England: La Roja have a 100% record in Group A3 but Thomas Tuchel’s side head into Sunday evening’s Madrid meeting with a chance of toppling them after securing a 2-1 victory against Croatia at Wembley. With Italy travelling to Belgium and France facing Turkey elsewhere, there’s plenty on his radar, notwithstanding three cracking WSL fixtures.

Turin hosts the world’s best eight men’s players, with the world No 1 Alexander Zverev getting the tournament under way on Sunday. He faces Spain’s Rafael Jódar, the first man to reach the ATP Finals in the same season he made his full ATP Tour debut. The German took top spot in the men’s rankings earlier this month after winning Roland Garros and the US Open – his first grand slam titles – and he is gunning for a third finals triumph. He is expected to win the four-man John McEnroe Group, while seven-time grand-slam winner Carlos Alcaraz heads up the Ivan Lendl Group after winning the Paris Masters. Tom Bassam live blogs the opener, and we’ll be back later to cover the evening’s matches.

Graham Searles tunes in to events unfurling in Munich, Bavaria, as the New England Patriots face the Detroit Lions. Sunday’s game will be the sixth regular-season match-up in Germany, a key market for the NFL in its aggressive international push. The Patriots (5-4) have lost two of their past three games and have many injury concerns, including running back Rhamondre Stevenson. Meanwhile, the Lions, despite a 6-2 record and four straight victories, are trying to keep pace in the tight NFC North. He’ll then move on to the seven 6pm fixtures.

While the Wallabies try to fix their porous defence, their hosts are trying to shore up their own rearguard as Murrayfield prepares for two sides in dire need of uplift. The problems faced by Les Kiss’s leaky mob were highlighted in the 45-22 thrashing at Twickenham by England. Australia, once the scourge of northern hemisphere sides, have now conceded 176 points in their past four Tests, the most ever over any equivalent quartet of matches in the Wallabies’ annals. Yet the same urgent repair job is being undertaken in the Scotland camp after Gregor Townsend’s side shipped 43 points to the All Blacks at their Edinburgh fortress last weekend. Daniel Gallan dons his scrum cap for live blog coverage.

Draw specialists Arsenal step up their hunt for a European berth after last weekend’s vital defeat of Liverpool and spirits lifted further by a creditable 1-1 draw in Barcelona in midweek. By contrast, Eder Maestre’s side are unbeaten in their past three away league matches, scoring 12 goals along the way. John Brewin is our MBM blog host, with Tom Garry reporting from the Emirates.

England wind up 2026 with the chance to top their Nations League group in Sunday’s collision with world champions Spain. Thomas Tuchel’s Three Lions were minutes away from securing a place in the World Cup final against Spain, who ran out 3-2 victors when they eventually did meet in September’s Nations League opener at Wembley. England will attempt to win the group, having secured their place in March’s Nations League quarter-finals with last month’s results. Harry Kane’s spot-kick settled things against Croatia on Thursday evening at Wembley after Petar Sucic cancelled out Morgan Rogers’ opener on a night when the England skipper became the most capped Englishman in history. Daniel Harris buckles up for the blog, with David Hytner and Sid Lowe reporting from Madrid.

#852. The beautiful game: revived art prize gives football its creative due once more | Emma John

Football and the art world have long remained distant but the breadth of entries for this year’s award reveals a healthy revival

It may be the Beautiful Game, but in its early decades football was a rare subject for artists. The Italian Futurist Umberto Boccioni whirled an athlete’s body into a vortex of movement in his 1913 painting Dynamism of a Soccer Player. You can see one of the earliest fine art depictions of a match – a smoggy, factory-adjactent scene called Any Wintry Afternoon in England – at the Manchester Art Gallery. If 1930s abstraction is more your thing, you can enjoy decoding the geometric shapes in Kazimir Malevich’s Painterly Realism of a Football Player – Color Masses in the 4th Dimension. I’m guessing the small green pea shape is a ball.

These, in any case, were exceptions. In 1953 the Football Association launched an art prize, backed by the newly formed Arts Council: the winning works included Going To The Match by LS Lowry, with its crowds flocking to Bolton Wanderers’ then home ground, Burnden Park. An exhibition of the submissions, Football and The Fine Arts, toured the country and the FA secretary, Sir Stanley Rous, said he hoped it would finally break the barrier between those two worlds.

Reader, it did not. But it did set a precedent that is being enthusiastically revived. It’s even possible that, after several decades of hurt, the world’s favourite sport may finally be getting its artistic due. There have been three iterations of the Football Art Prize in the past 20 years, and the latest arrives at the National Football Museum this month (from the Sheffield Millennium Gallery) with a breadth of entries that demonstrate how resonant the subject can be.

Meticulous still lives – of battered balls, or boots mid-clean – ache with memory. There’s haunting photo-documentary: Bangladeshi youths playing a pickup game in the middle of a rubbish dump, pitches affected by climate change. “You see the whole gamut of footballing experience on display,” says the museum’s exhibitions director, Pip Diment. Her assumptions – she initially imagined herself hanging portraits of famous moments and iconic players – were overturned. “Pretty much every one of the artists is expressing how football matters to them, but they’re responding and reacting in such different ways.”

There are a few famous faces nevertheless. One artist worked in charcoals to create a hyper-realist bust of N’Golo Kanté. Roy Keane appears twice, once proffering a plate of prawn sandwiches to his viewer, another time in a diptych with Micah Richards. The latter is the work of Conor Rogers, whose satirical series of paintings on abandoned betting slips took second prize. They include a poignant image of Sheffield United’s manager, Chris Wilder, head in hands, next to a repurposed bookmaker’s logo asking: “Lad r u ok?”

Diment says football and art are still perceived as almost entirely separate spheres, so it’s interesting that this year’s winning work – a video by Alina Akbar – explores the connection between “high” and “popular” culture. In Footwork, the multimedia artist segues between keepy-uppy skills and the choreographed movements of Kathak, an Indian classical dance style. The combined rhythms and sounds create a mesmerising meditation on identity, related to the northern South Asian community in which she grew up.

Football, she says, is a post-migration culture whose value is sometimes overlooked by the very people who adopted it. “Whenever I went to my great-grandparents’ house, football was on TV all the time and I’d be on their street, trying out tricks,” says Akbar. “My grandad and his brothers were really excited when I started playing, because they’d gone through the more racist era of the 70s, and they never went to games.”

For all its social themes, Akbar’s work still expresses the balletic movement and poise that Picasso once pursued in the flowing form of his ceramic sculpture Footballeur. It’s interesting how so much of the art in the show reflects football culture rather than the game itself – watching from the sofa, in the pub, on the touchline of a recreational game. Perhaps it’s hard for artists to compete with the volume of visual content that the games already provide. And we have moved a long way from a classically inspired fascination with athletes’ physiques (for comparison, check out the leaping goalkeeper in Cecil Beaton’s mid-20th-century painting Footballers, with his unashamedly pert buttocks).

Tim Marlow, the director of the Design Museum and chair of the judging panel, points out that “artists today have unashamedly adopted the position of the spectator or the fan” and that it’s rare to find works that try to get inside the experience of the footballer themselves. One of his favourite exceptions is the 2006 film, Zidane: A 21st Century Portrait, which he calls “a great piece of conceptual art”. “It’s a really intimate study of the game, which in the current era, when you’ve got referees with head cams, might feel old hat, but nothing like it had been done before.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

And then there’s Tottenham’s stadium gallery, OOF, where exhibitions of football-related work have ranged from Roger Mayne’s 1950s street photography to AC Larsen’s polemic on the FA’s trans ban. This month brought the opening of Trackie McLeod’s celebration of Wag culture. Historic football art, meanwhile, is rocketing in value. Four years ago Lowry’s Going To The Match went for £7.8m at auction, a record price for the Salford artist’s work, and in 2022 one of Nicholas de Staël’s Parc des Princes 1952 abstract series – based on a friendly he watched between France and Sweden – became the most expensive football artwork when it sold for £16.7m.

Money has always been a key element in the art world, and there are notable collectors within the footballing world today, from billionaire club owners to cultured former players. Fabio Capello has a well documented passion for Kandinsky; David Beckham’s collection is said to include Andy Warhol, Banksy and Yayoi Kusama; Michael Ballack is spotted at major art fairs around the world. The whimsically named J St John, who organised Football and Fine Arts, told the Liverpool Daily Post 70 years ago that art needed a new form of patronage, to help people appreciate the painted canvas in the same they understood the artistry of Joe Mercer, Ferenc Puskas and Stanley Matthews. Could his dream finally be coming to pass?

#851. Record-breaking Ebola outbreak: phone data reconstruct first weeks of spread

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Confirmed infections of Bundibugyo Ebola have surpassed 10,000 in the DRC since May.Credit: Xinhua/Shutterstock

Epidemiologists have used mobile-phone data and test records to map the early spread of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC)1 weeks before the outbreak was declared. The authors say the study findings reveal how surveillance systems failed to detect signals of the disease early on and enabled it to spread rapidly.

It is now six months since the outbreak of the Bundibugyo strain of the virus was announced. The number of confirmed infections has risen to more than 10,000 and 5,198 people have died, making this the largest Bundibugyo outbreak so far. There are no licenced vaccines or approved treatments specifically for Bundibugyo, which has complicated efforts to control it.

The DRC declared the outbreak on 15 May after laboratory tests confirmed the first case, a person from Ituri province in the country’s northeast, was infected with the Bundibugyo strain. Around the same time, suspected cases were being reported in several DRC locations, including Mongbwalu, Rwampara, Bunia and Nyankunde in Ituri, and Butembo, Katwa and Goma in the neighbouring province of North Kivu. The World Health Organization declared the outbreak a public health emergency of international concern on 17 May, citing infections among health-care workers, the geographical spread of cases and clusters of undocumented deaths. Researchers strongly suspect that the virus had been spreading in the region months earlier.

To understand how the outbreak spread so quickly, the researchers looked at anonymized mobile-phone data to trace the movement of people between areas.

Although the first confirmed case was identified on 15 May, the study reports that the person had symptoms as early as 25 April.

The team found that people travelling out of Mongbwalu, Bunia and Rwampara between 24 April and 24 May helped to predict which health zones would report infections by 1 June. For instance, areas close to the initial centres were at greater risk of infections, the study found.

The risk of infections rose again in places 150–200 kilometres away from the initial outbreak centres because people travelled to larger towns and cities along established routes, says study co-author Pierre Akilimali, an epidemiologist at the National Institute of Public Health (INSP) in Kinshasa.

The authors say the findings show that people movement was a key driver of the rapid spread in the early phases of the outbreak.

“These are very important findings which reinforce what we initially knew at the onset of the outbreak,” says Tambe Akem, an independent public-health consultant based in Yaoundé, Cameroon.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03666-z

#849. Collin Gosselin Reveals His Hope to Have Kids

In the Shadow of Eight: Surviving the Reality of My Childhood author Collin Gosselin exclusively shared with E! News what his hopes are for his future, including where he stands on having kids.

Collin Gosselin is looking to his future.

While the Special Forces season five winner is grateful for what he’s achieved in his life as an advocate for children and those in need, he does have an idea of what he thinks could be better than this.

“The one thing that could top this beautiful mission I'm on is probably being a father,” Gosselin exclusively shared with E! News, “but I feel so young. I've already found something so great and so meaningful, and to that I am very fortunate.”

And so much of that mission crystallized for the 22-year-old in his memoir In the Shadow of Eight: Surviving the Reality of My Childhood—which is currently a New York Times No.1 best seller and has been nominated for favorite memoir and audiobook in the Goodreads Choice Awards.

The release of Gosselin’s book has allowed him to reach new audiences, many of whom have been moved by his vulnerability as he discussed growing up in the public eye on the reality series Jon & Kate Plus 8 with parents Jon Gosselin and Kate Gosselin, as well as his fellow sextuplets Alexis, Leah, Joel, Hannah and Aaden, and 26-year-old twin sisters Mady and Cara.

“The coolest, the most meaningful messages I've got from people are them sharing their stories with me,” Gosselin told E!. “Talking about their dynamics with their parents and their siblings and their childhoods. And people I've never met before having that vulnerability? That's hard to do.”

Even he himself was nervous about being so vulnerable regarding his life in his memoir, adding, “That's scary to do.”

“But now, they're coming back to me, they're messaging me and they're sharing their stories with me,” he said, “and I'm like, Wow.’ I know it doesn't sound crazy, but to me it's really crazy because I know how scary it is to wanna open up.”

And that fact that so many people felt comfortable “choosing to do that with” him felt incredibly empowering and helped Gosselin learn how true emotional healing can happen.

“I’ve started this cycle of people choosing to talk about their emotions, to be vulnerable, and to talk about things that they're scared to talk about,” he explained, “and that's how healing happens. That's how we heal, is by talking about things.”

And despite a difficult childhood, Gosselin found that it inspired the mission he’s now on, saying, “The greatest thing is that what has happened in my past—as hard as it was—it has given me a purpose to do something greater with my life.”

For a look at all the difficult moments Gosselin wrote about in his memoir, keep reading.

Collin Gosselin Says His Mom Separated Him From His Siblings

On a 2015 episode of Kate Plus 8—the Jon & Kate Plus 8 spinoff Kate Gosselin  led following her 2009 divorce from Jon Gosselin—TLC viewers watched as twins Mady Gosselin and Cara Gosselin moved into their own rooms in Kate's 7,500-square-foot estate, while their younger sisters Leah Gosselin, Alexis Gosselin and Hannah Gosselin inhabited a shared upstairs room and brothers Collin Gosselin, Joel Gosselin and Aaden Gosselin made over a basement space.

"It was like a slumber party every night," Collin recounts of that first week in his memoir Shadow of Eight: Surviving the Reality of My Childhood. "Then, one day, I was told by my mom I’d be moving out. An air mattress appeared in the unfinished part of the basement, shoved into the far back corner like an afterthought."

Coming on the heels of him being cut out of weekend visits with his dad (he was told Jon didn't want to see him; Jon was told the opposite) and frequently isolated (he recalls one night where he was sent to bed while his siblings watched TV with Kate), having to live next to their deep freezers felt particularly cold.

"I was part of a plan," he notes of the punishments, he attributed to his unwillingness to play ball on camera "I just didn’t know what it was."

E! News reached out to reps for Kate and TLC about the accusations in Collin's book and has not heard back. However, this past June, Kate referred to her son's accusations as "ridiculous" in the comment section of her TikTok page.

Collin Gosselin Claims His Parents Kate Gosselin and Jon Gosselin Were Offered Millions to Stay Married

As Jon and Kate's marriage began to unravel, claims Collin, Dr. Phil host Phil McGraw was teaming with TLC "to negotiate a deal to keep their marriage together for cameras."

So, when the couple shared their plans to divorce in January 2009, writes Collin, "the network responded by offering my parents $2 million to stay in the marriage and pretend the relationship was intact for the sake of the show’s longevity." Turning down the offer, Jon told the Daily Mail in 2019, "I couldn't live with myself. I couldn't live a lie."

E! News reached out to reps for Kate and TLC, but they did not respond. They also declined to comment on Daily Mail's previous story. A rep for McGraw called the allegations "false" in a statement to Us Weekly. Noting the talk show host didn't have "any direct or indirect interest, financial or otherwise," in the series, the rep added, "Neither Dr. Phil, nor anyone associated with his show ever facilitated, encouraged, participated in or knew anything about any payments to the Gosselins by the other network as alleged by their son Collin, who Dr. Phil has never met."

Collin Gosselin Says He Spent 70 Percent of His Time Locked in His Basement Bedroom

According to Collin, some 14 complaints were made against his mom to Children and Youth Services, one of them coming after he turned up to his fourth-grade classroom with a noticeably injured ear.

Not long after, "my mom pulled me from school," he wrote. "She told me it was temporary. That it was for my own good. That people were 'asking questions' and we needed to keep things calm for a while. I didn’t argue or ask how long. I'd learned that asking questions made things worse."

Collin said he was also banned from playing with the family's LEGO sets. But perhaps the biggest change, Collin alleged, was the walls Kate had built around his basement air mattress with two security cameras he had to speak through if he needed to be let out to use the bathroom.

"Most days, I spent about 70 percent of my time locked in that room," writes Collin. "The rest was split between meeting with my teacher, eating alone without my siblings, cleaning up after everyone or pretending to be happy when the cameras came around. That was my life."

Collin Gosselin Claims Mom Kate Gosselin Told His Siblings He Was a Bad Kid

To explain why Collin was no longer attending school with them or even joining the rest of the family to eat dinner, Kate would tell his siblings he was troubled, Collin writes.

"'Collin needs more help than you kids,' she would say right in front of me," he details in his book. "'You and your friends at school aren't bad like your brother.' They were repeatedly told that I was unpredictable, violent, beyond help. They grew up around me as if I was a cautionary tale. They were children themselves. How could they know to doubt her?"

Kate previously told People that Collin received "multiple psychiatric diagnoses" and inpatient psychiatric treatment in response to "unpredictable and violent behavior." But Jon claimed to the Daily Mail in 2019 that Collin had no known diagnosed medical condition other than common ADHD.

Collin Gosselin Alleges Mom Kate Gosselin Once Bound His Wrists and Ankles With Zip Ties

Having tired of his basement existence by age 11, Collin plotted his escape, using his twin-size air mattress to climb out the tiny basement window. But with nowhere to go—"It had been almost two years since I'd seen my dad"—he returned home.

Once there, his mattress was gone, as were the few books he had. Then, Collin detailed, Kate allegedly came in with zip ties for his wrists and ankles.

"Once I was bound, she grabbed me by my wrists, pulled me up into a standing position and then threw me down, slamming my tailbone against the hard floor," Collin alleges, adding she told him he was a burden to the family. "She went on, calling me crazy, dangerous and other names nobody should ever call a child, things that stuck long after the pain faded."

A rep for Kate didn’t respond to E! News' request for comment. But her attorney previously told The Sun, "There's always two sides to every story and when things take place in the past, it's hard to determine because people have differing recollections and perspectives."

However, his take, he added, was "if Kate did the things that Collin is accusing Kate of, she would have been investigated by the authorities and prosecuted."

Collin Gosselin Recounts Being Physically Restrained and Sedated at a Mental Health Clinic

After his escape attempt, Collin claims he was transported to Fairmount Behavioral Health System mere days before his 12th birthday. Throughout his 21-month stay in the mental health clinic—where most kids stayed just days or weeks, he claims—he was given daily medication. "My brain had started feeling soft and cloudy, like someone had turned a dimmer switch down," he details. "I found myself zoning out, feeling like a zombie."

During one incident, 18 months into his stay, Collin alleges he was physically restrained and injected with a medication he dubbed "booty juice" after asking administrators why he was still there. After another, a staffer bent his wrist in such a way that "a violent, searing pain shot up my arm, so intense it made my knees buckle." (E! News reached out to Fairmount Behavioral Health System, but has not heard back.)

Throughout his nearly two-year stay, Collin says his mom visited once.

Collin Gosselin Says He Smuggled a Letter to Dad Jon Gosselin to Get Out of the Mental Health Clinic

With his mom and siblings no longer taking his calls from Fairmount, said Collin, he hatched a plan to reconnect with his dad. After hitting it off with one of his roommates, Collin confided in him about his reality star past.

Writing a letter to his father in crayon while hiding in a bathroom stall, Collin claimed he asked his roommate to find a way to deliver it. Soon after, he was discharged to a residential facility where he was able to once-again attend school and slowly weaned off his medications.

It was there that he connected with his dad for the first time, Jon sharing in that initial phone call that he had plans to bring him home.

As Jon later detailed to Collin—who ended up moving in with him, sister Hannah and Jon's then-girlfriend Colleen Conrad—he had spent years trying to track him down. Then he received Collin's letter and filed an emergency petition with the court to modify custody.

Collin Gosselin Says He Hasn't Seen Most of His Siblings Since He Was 15

Other than Hannah, Collin has only seen his siblings once since leaving Kate's home at age 11—a court-mandated visit just before his 15th birthday. "It was a way to keep the kids together, despite being split between two households," Collin reasons, noting the meet-up started out awkwardly before they all teamed up to best the amusement center's games.

But, as Leah, Alexis, Joel and Aaden moved toward the exit, "No one turned back," Collin recounts. "And I haven't seen them since."

#848. How Ferguson-inspired Pochettino can succeed where Carrick failed at Man Utd

Maurucio Pochettino (right) was first mentioned as a contender to manage Manchester United when Louis van Gaal was sacked in May 2016

When Mauricio Pochettino was asked the three Premier League managers he would have loved to have played for, he was unequivocal.

"Sir Alex Ferguson, Sir Alex Ferguson, Sir Alex Ferguson," replied Pochettino, who on Friday was named Manchester United manager.

In 2023, the Argentine - then at Chelsea, and dressed in full Blues training gear - was being interviewed by Sky Sports. Still he felt a need to express his adoration for Ferguson.

Six years prior to that interview, while managing Tottenham, he had shared lunch with the legendary former United manager.

"When I was young, when I started my career as a manager, he was always my inspiration, my reference," Pochettino said.

"And when you can share two hours with a person who was the greatest manager in the history of football, you can only enjoy."

Hiring United managers has been complicated since Ferguson's departure in 2013, and one of the most prominent complications has been a back-and-forth around the club's DNA.

For some, winning by any means necessary should take precedence, while others believe the style of play and cultural heritage of United's most successful period is vital to the club's identity.

In recent years, United's managerial merry-go-round has alternated between European coaches with their own fixed styles of play, and former players from the Ferguson era.

But between his tactics of choice and his adoration for the former United boss, Pochettino may be uniquely placed to bridge the gap between both camps.

Pochettino a decade in Man Utd's making - but Carrick deserves better

Michael Carrick's United produced a series of good results to finish last season with a run unmatched by any other team in the league. They looked great, but it was a greatness built on attacking in a transition-heavy manner.

Under Carrick, in games they had less than 50% of the ball, they only lost once. In those 13 games, they boasted a win-rate of 62%. This dropped to 36% in games they had the majority of possession.

This style of play suited their direct attackers and protected their defenders.

At the same time, Casemiro's set-piece prowess provided United a reliable way to break the deadlock against deep defences - something they have struggled with this season.

With United a goal up, opponents stepped forward, giving Carrick's men more space. They could play to their strengths again, attacking quickly. It worked.

But teams at the top are reluctant to play in this way. Carrick's vision for United was a side that played slick football, with short passes in build-up intuitively, referencing Paris St-Germain's midfield three as a source of inspiration.

Building up in this manner, to entice and escape from pressure, before looking to find the forwards quickly, was the plan Carrick was working towards.

This didn't come to fruition and trying to take United from a successful counter-attacking side to one that could reliably beat teams while keeping the ball was the same hurdle that undid Ole Gunnar Solskjar and Erik ten Hag.

Former players under Sir Alex Ferguson, both Ole Gunnar Solskjar and Michael Carrick leaned into Unitedâs historic style when crafting their game-models

Pochettino gives United an interesting solution to this problem.

In his own words, he has described his sides as needing "to be protagonists, always press high, work hard and be dynamic". He refers to himself as a "disciple" of the legendary Argentina boss Marcelo Bielsa, who he played for.

If you wanted an immediate comparison in the Premier League to a coach who resembles Pochettino's ideas in possession, it would be worth looking at Liverpool's Andoni Iraola, who similarly cites Bielsa as his reference.

These are coaches who, while taking the initiative, encourage vertical football. For as different as the clubs are, both the fans of United and Liverpool have enjoyed success when their teams have played high-octane football.

This summer's World Cup was a strong showcase of Pochettino's style of play and his recent tactical adaptation.

Rather than a fixed, positional style of play - akin to the work of somebody like Manchester City's Enzo Maresca - Pochettino's USA had only certain players being tasked with holding their position.

This approach posed problems for teams who defended in a zonal manner - defending specific areas rather than individual players.

The US midfielders being able to move freely meant they could step into areas of the pitch between the zones that were being defended, which resulted in their players often being unmarked with time and space on the ball.

By playing in close proximity to each other in the middle of the pitch, the US found another benefit.

Small-space passing combinations helped draw the opposing team up towards the ball and combined with clever off-ball movement to stretch the pitch, allowed the US to find their striker with few defenders around him.

Pochettino's men looked to thread through-balls in behind and early after enticing the opposition's press and the speedy Folarin Balogun was able to turn those chances into goals.

Here is a good example of USA's fluid midfield four under Pochettino. The right-sided midfielder McKennie has placed himself near his three midfield team-mates, leaving the right half-space empty. With a four against three in that area of the pitch, USA are best placed to play quick combinations before looking to find their attackers in space.

Here we can see the swapping of left-winger Pulisic and left-back Robinsonâs positions. In this example, Robinson inverts into the fluid midfield four with Pulisic positioned on the touchline for balance. When out wide, Pulisic was able to showcase impressive one-against-one dribbling throughout the match too.

This combination of a fluid midfield, small-space passing and direct through-balls doesn't sound dissimilar to what Carrick was trying to move towards implementing this season.

And although that may worry United fans, the similarity in principles will benefit the players.

"My philosophy is to give a freer style with a good organisation," were Pochettino's words in 2014.

Although philosophically similar, that latter part - a clearer organisation to his freer style - is likely to be what Carrick was unable to reliably offer his players.

For fans of top sides, fast-paced, vertical football tends to be accepted when it comes from a place of being proactive - think Ferguson's United or Jurgen Klopp's Liverpool - wanting to keep the ball, but not passing it for passing's sake.

Fast-paced, vertical football tends to be frowned upon when it comes from a place of conceding possession and defending your own goal for long periods of the match.

The first half of Carrick's stint did appear proactive, while his 4-2-4 press worked well. Leaving four players high was a risk that allowed them to win the ball back and score quickly, but as teams figured this out, United failed to adapt.

There also appeared to be a drop in the team's fitness the longer United went from the departure of ex-boss Ruben Amorim, who left United well conditioned, albeit on the back of a schedule without European football.

Here we see United's narrow 4-2-4 defensive shape in the first half against Como

Hiring Pochettino will immediately begin the process of turning United into a well-drilled side, capable of applying intense pressure, likely in a co-ordinated manner.

Pochettino enjoyed relative success with Spurs, built on this intensity and co-ordination, that differentiated him from the rest of the league.

With that unique selling point more common now than a decade ago, how he builds on it will dictate how his tenure unfolds.

But watching Brighton this season, he can be assured that an approach founded on intensity off the ball can work in the Premier League in 2026, with Fabian Hurzeler's men second in the league, with the fourth highest average possession, 10 games in.

Pochettino, from a footballing point of view, feels extremely aligned to the values of Ferguson's United, and as a result will implement numerous similarities to the things Carrick wanted, but ultimately failed, to deliver.

His wealth of experience make him a more proven entity than the departing United manager and if he can get his team fit and pressing high, in typically Pochettino fashion, they should see an upturn in form.

Expanding on his managerial approach, while managing Spurs he explained how "the most important thing [was] to create a good shape for players to be comfortable and to show their real qualities".

Rather than relying on pre-defined pattern, he looks to empower individuals to solve attacking problems. Taking this approach means recruitment of top talent matters more than ever.

"He [gave] me the confidence and licence to go where I wanted on the pitch, where I [could] use my strengths," said Cole Palmer, who enjoyed his most productive Premier League season under Pochettino at Chelsea.

United have good attackers but they will need to take the same initiative Palmer did, if platformed to their strengths - something Pochettino does well.

If they don't, and if Pochettino is to stumble, it will likely be in United's inability to break down stubborn defences when asked to dominate the ball - in what would feel like Groundhog Day, again.
